newsitem.title: USA: IBM tumbles on estimate cuts, currency woes.
newsitem.headline: IBM tumbles on estimate cuts, currency woes.

text.p: Shares of International Business Machines Corp tumbled after three different analysts made negative comments in the past two days, saying that a stronger dollar and a product transition will hurt earnings.

IBM shares were off 2-3/4 to $133-7/8 in heavy trading. On Thursday, both Merrill Lynch and Dean Witter analysts made negative comments about IBM, with Dean Witter cutting estimates. Then Friday, Morgan Stanley cut earnings estimates.
"People are beginning to realize that it's going to be a bleak quarter," said Jay Stevens, a Dean Witter analyst. Stevens maintained his accumulate rating on the computer giant.

Analysts said two main factors were hurting IBM's earnings prospects. Though the computer giant will have a lower tax rate and fewer shares outstanding due to a share buyback plan, currency fluctuations and anticipation of some sluggishness in mainframe sales will hurt the first half of 1997.

Stevens of Dean Witter cut his first half estimates by $0.10 and added $0.05 to his second half estimates, resulting in a net estimate cut of $0.05 to $12.25 a share for 1997, down from $12.30 a share previously.
"We view the year as more back-end loaded," said Steve Milunovich, a Morgan Stanley analyst, who also cut numbers.

Back-end loaded means that more earnings and revenues are expected in the second half of the year. Milunovich said a product transtition to a faster mainframe model will likely cause some malaise among current IBM mainframe customers.
"Some users may wait for the new one," Milunovich said.

Analysts said IBM is expected to upgrade its low-cost CMOS (complementary metal oxide semiconductor) mainframes to faster processors with estimated processing power of 60-65 MIPS (million instructions per second). This would bring the CMOS family to the same performance level as the high end of its older bi-polar line, which IBM is phasing out.
Currently, the fastest CMOS processors are 45 MIPS.
"This is a major product transition," Stevens said.
Analysts have been expecting initial shipments of the new CMOS processors in the third quarter. Milunovich said he expects a few models will be shipped in June.

Daniel Mandresh of Merrill Lynch said Thursday in a note to clients that he expects demand will be extremely good for these machines and he expects IBM to beat Wall Street's expectations of initial shipments in the third quarter. But until then, the stronger dollar overseas will continue to weigh on earnings.

Mandresh said he is expecting a hit of roughly $0.20 a share from currency, which he said will neutralize a $0.16 a share benefit from the company's stock buyback. He estimates that IBM's current shares outstanding will decline by 38 million shares, due to its ongoing share buyback program.
As of the end of the fourth quarter, IBM had an average of $513.4 million common shares outstanding.

Mandresh did not change his current first quarter estimate of $2.32 a share. But he said that he is looking for three percent revenue growth in the first quarter and a tough comparison versus a year ago.
